section: 3. Creating objects with the assignment operator <-
text:
3. Creating objects with the assignment operator <-
An important feature of R is to create objects.
Objects are used to store a variety of values: numbers, lists, entire datasets, and more. Storing these values as objects allows us to use them again and again, without retyping them.
We create objects using the assignment operator: <- , which is a less than sign, <, followed by a minus sign, -.

text:
4. Using Functions & Arguments
Functions are small programs inside R that perform tasks for us. R comes with many built-in functions like summary(), mean(), and plot().
Arguments are the inputs you provide to a function to customize its behavior or to provide the data on which it operates.
For example, we can create a plot of the objects that we created earlier (i.e., a & a2) using the plot() function. We will use arguments to tell the plot() function what we want it to use as the x-axis and the y-axis:








Fancier arguments can tell the function, for example, what kind of plot we want, what color we want to make the plot, or whether we want to include descriptive labels and titles. Let’s use, for example, the col argument to change the color:









Help pages
Whenever you want to learn more about a function, you can use ?functionname, as in the code below. Please note that reading documentation pages is another skill on its own that develops over time.

5. Packages
Many functions of R live in packages. Packages are similar to apps on your phone. Your phone is powerful as is, but you can make it more powerful and add new features to it by installing new apps. Similarly, R is strong as is, but we can add new functions to it by installing new packages.
Today, we will use a package called palmerpenguins, so we will install it using the following line of code:








After we install a package, we have to call it using the library() so that we can use the functions that come with it.














Important



You need to install a package only once, but to use its functions, you need to always call it using library().

title: The Tidyverse Workflow for Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualization in R
text:
These are the stickers you will receive at the end of the workshop! 🙂

Logistics

Today’s activities are web-based; that is, you do not need to download any software. R will magically run in your browser! When you use R on your own, you will need the following software: R and RStudio. At the end of the workshop, you will be given resources to help you (a) install these software and (b) become familiar with their interface.
You can edit the code chunks in any way you want. When you want a code chunk to return to its original state, just click on “Start Over.”
If you refresh the page, you will lose your progress, so at the end of each page, you may want to print your progress as a PDF file.



Objectives
By the end of the workshop, you will be able to

identify some key functions of R
define foundational R terminology such as object, function, package, library, and argument
summarize numerical variables using descriptive statistics such as mean, standard deviation, min, max, and median (resources for categorical variables will be provided but not covered in the workshop)
visualize data in scatter plots and box plots (resources for bar plots and histograms will be provided but not covered in the workshop)
“wrangle” data by dropping NA observations, creating new variables based on existing variables, and filtering data based on desired parameters



Rough Schedule

1 PM - 2:45 PM: Introductions and the tabs The Foundation and Descriptives & Data Wrangling
2:45 PM - 3:00 PM: 15-min break
3:00 PM - 5:00 PM: The last three tabs Visualizations Part I, Visualizations Part II, Moving Forward

text:
1. Defining the required elements
Every plot we create with ggplot2 requires the ggplot() function. When we run ggplot() on its own, it creates an empty, gray square—a blank canvas for us to do our “art”! Let’s see it in action.








We need to add some arguments to ggplot() if we want to plot data. Arguments are the information we give to a function to change how the function behaves.
Let’s plot body_mass_g and flipper_length_mm. To do so, we will need the following:

the data argument to supply a dataset and
the mapping argument to connect variables from the dataset to visual properties (i.e., aesthetics) of the plot.







Your turn!
Fill in the following code chunk to supply the data penguins and map body_mass_g to the x-axis and flipper_length_mm to the y-axis.











We still have not plotted the data, though. The function geom_point() will add a scatter plot layer to our plot.






Your turn!
Copy your code from above and then add + geom_point(). Then, run the code chunk to see the result.











The + operator combines ggplot2 functions. Without the +, R doesn’t know that you want to add geom_point() to the plot you started with ggplot(). Missing the + operator or putting it on a new line are common errors people receive when using ggplot2.

Template for ggplot():
ggplot(data = DATAFRAME, mapping = aes(x = VARIABLE, y = VARIABLE)) + geom_point()


ggplot() initiates a blank canvas where we can create our plot
data supplies the dataset
aes() determines which variable should be on the x-axis and which on the y-axis
geom_point() adds a scatter plot layer







Your turn!
Using the template above, create a scatter plot to show the relationship between bill_length_mm (x-axis) and bill_depth_mm (y-axis). Write your code from scratch without copying and pasting 🙂

















Your turn!

2. Customizing plots by changing aesthetics
Visual aspects like the color, shape, and size are called aesthetics.
The following code, for example, changes the color aesthetic for the scatter points. Run the code to see the result.














Your turn!
Edit the code below to turn the points “maroon” instead.











ggplot2 recognizes a range of color names. Run the function colors() to see a list of options.








The following table contains some aesthetics that you can use with geom_point():








Aesthetic
What it controls
Use




color
Color
Quoted name of a color, e.g., “blue”


size
Size
Number


shape
Shape (circle, triangle, etc.)
An integer between 0 and 25


alpha
Transparency
A number between 0 and 1

alpha = 1 creates completely opaque points.
alpha = 0 creates completely transparent ones.

Setting alpha less than 1 helps with overplotting.

text:
4. Layering geoms
So far, we have learned how to use geom_point() together with ggplot(), but with ggplot, we can add multiple geoms to one plot. Let’s add a regression line to our scatter plot by adding geom_smooth().








What do you think will happen if we add color = species inside aes() in ggplot()? 🕵️‍♀️ Hint: Any aesthetics in ggplot() will apply to all the geoms that follow.


Global aesthetics—applying aesthetics to all geoms that follow
This one applies the color aesthetic mapping to both geom_point() and geom_smooth().










Local aesthetics—applying aesthetics to a specific geom
This one applies the color aesthetic mapping only to geom_point().








This one applies the color aesthetic mapping only to geom_smooth().










Regression line
geom_smooth defaults to the loess method for the regression line, but you can change that to the linear model by changing the method argument to lm.

text:
1. Setup
Remember that we have to install packages only once, but we always have to call them into our workspace using library().











2. Box plots
We can use box plots to show the distribution of a numerical variable broken down by a categorical variable (e.g., body mass by species).
With box plots, we need to tell R what variable goes on the x and y axes. The y-axis is for the numerical variable while the x-axis is for the categorical grouping variable.
Let’s examine body_mass_g across different species using geom_boxplot():








Let’s also give each species a different color by mapping the fill argument to the variable species














Your turn!
Add onto the code below to recreate the plot below. Hint: fill and facet_grid.















3. Histograms (For you to look at later)
We can use histograms to examine the distribution of values for a numerical variable. With histograms, we only need the x variable. y is created automatically and shows the counts.
Let’s create a histogram for body_mass_g using geom_histogram():








We can color the bins to be able to see them more clearly:

color -> Color the outlines of bins
fill -> Color the inside of the bins









We can also change the number of bins with bins or the width of the bins with binwidth:














Your turn!
Update the code below so that we can see how body_mass_g values are distributed across the levels of the sex variable.
You can either map the variable sex to fill OR use facet_wrap().














4. Bar plots (For you to look at later)
Similar to histograms, we only need to provide x, which will be the categorical variable of interest. y will be automatically calculated and indicate how many observations fall into each category.
Let’s count how many penguins we have in each species:














Your turn!
How can we color the species differently?












Stacked bar plots
We can also use bar plots to show how one categorical variable is distributed within another categorical variable. To do this, we map one categorical variable to x and another to fill.










Side-by-side bar plots
If stacked bar plots are hard to compare, we can place the bars next to each other using position = "dodge".










Standardized bar plots
Sometimes we want to compare proportions instead of counts. We can do so with position = "fill". Now, each bar will have the same height, and the breakdown will show the proportion of each subgroup.














Your turn!
Create a stacked bar plot with species on the x-axis. Each bar should represent the total count of penguins for that species, with different fill colors indicating the island they come from.














5. Further customizing your plots
Using ggplot2, you can customize pretty much any aspect of your plot. Here are two popular tools:

themes control the overall appearance of the plot such as the background, grid lines, and text size
scales control how colors are assigned to variables such as fill colors and outline colors


Themes
Let’s start with a basic box plot:








We can now apply a theme to it.

Because species is mapped to fill, we can use the scale_fill_manual() function to control the colors:








Instead of manually selecting colors, we can also use a built-in palette with scale_fill_brewer().








Click here to see all palettes.






If our variable of interest was mapped to the color aesthetic, then we would use scale_color_manual and scale_color_brewer.
